title: Quantum Mosaic capacity needs synthesis
summary: High-level qualification for dedicated capacity. Customer runs latency sensitive multi-tenant inference for document retrieval and RAG; wants reserved GPUs with strict isolation and ability to burst for traffic spikes. Security and KMS, audit logs and SOC 2 are gating. Agreed next step: pilot (2 reserved nodes, benchmark week), Redwood to share pricing + burst model and security pack.
action_items: Maya Chen - Send pricing sheet and burst-model template - due 2026-09-03
Omar Reyes - Provision benchmark test plan + initial perf script for customer's 512-token RAG workload - due 2026-09-01
Priya Nair - Share recent traffic spikes CSV and sample prompt set (anonymized) - due 2026-08-31
next_steps: Redwood to send security pack (SOC2 summary, SSO/SAML notes, KMS integration guide)
Schedule 1-week pilot with 2 reserved nodes (preferred regions: us-east-1)
Set up a 60m bench session to run 95th percentile latency and tail tail tests
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-28 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~44m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Reyes (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO - Quantum Mosaic), Liam O'Connor (Infra Lead), Sara Patel (ML Eng), Benji Rao (Product)

Summary (auto): Qualified for Dedicated reserved GPU. Needs strict tenant isolation, fast cold-starts for burtsy traffic, and SOC 2 / KMS compatibility. Pilot and pricing requested.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE for Redwood Inference. Uh Omar from our SE team is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya Nair: Hi, good thanks. We got a bunch of folks on from infra and product so we can cover both the technicals and the business bits.
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: Morning. Quick note, we're on a tight procurement window, Q4 budget, so timeline matters.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Understood. High level, we want to make sure dedicated makes sense for your SLOs and cost profile. Omar, want to do a quick run on their workload?
[00:25] Omar Reyes: Sure. Priya, could you give us the workloads at a WW level — RAG, embedding traffic, concurrency, typical token lengths?
[00:32] Priya Nair: Yeah. We're mostly running document retrieval RAG for user-facing search. Average prompt round trip is 350 tokens, but sometimes up to 1k. We have peaks during release windows and on product launches — spikes can be 6-8x baseline for a couple hours. Concurrency baseline 40 qps, peak 300 qps.
[00:50] Sara Patel: And a lot of multi-tenant calls, each tenant needs logical isolation — can't cross-leak caches. Also we have PII so encryption in flight and at rest and KMS key separation is required.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Got it. So isolation + strong key management. On the isolation front, Redwood Dedicated can provision reserved pools with tenant fencing and optional single-tenant nodes. For KV cache, we do logical partitioning and you can opt for node-level isolation if you need full blast radius reduction.
[01:20] Liam O'Connor: Quick question — how fast can we scale when there's a surge? We can't have cold-starts adding 500ms to tails.
[01:27] Omar Reyes: Two levers: warm pools (prewarmed containers/GPU instances) and burst capacity where we spill into shared burst with lower isolation guarantees. For reserved capacity you can configure a warm pool to keep X prewarmed instances which helps tail latency. The tradeoff is cost.
[01:42] Benji Rao: So is there a way to keep, like, a minimal warm pool and still handle a 6x spike without paying for 6x reserved all the time?
[01:50] Omar Reyes: Yes, you set a baseline of reserved nodes sized for normal concurrency and combine that with a warm pool and a short-lived burst buffer. In many customer patterns we recommend 1.5-2x baseline reserved and warm pool sized for the 95th percentile of expected burst duration, with a fallback to shared nodes for extreme spikes.
[02:10] Priya Nair: Hmm. We've got a compliance ask: any time we spill to shared nodes we need audit logs and end-to-end encryption under our KMS. Does Redwood support that?
[02:20] Maya Chen: We do support customer-managed KMS for private deployments and Dedicated as an option — you can route keys through your cloud KMS. For hosted/shared bursts, we can provide envelope encryption and access logs; however, some customers prefer Private for full key separation.
[02:34] Liam O'Connor: So maybe Private is worth considering; we do want to avoid any shared-KV cache scenario for certain tenants.
[02:40] Sara Patel: Also model determinism — can we pin model versions per tenant? We need reproducible outputs for a subset of tenants.
[02:46] Omar Reyes: Yes, you can pin model versions and freeze rollout policies. That works for both Dedicated and Private. One nuance: quantized variants might change outputs slightly so we recommend eval sets pre-deployment.
[02:58] Priya Nair: Cost sensitivity: we've modeled hosted per-token and it looks cheap at low volume but for our baseline and peaks, dedicated probably wins. We want a price sheet for reserved nodes and the burst model.
[03:10] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We'll share a detailed pricing sheet and a burst-simulation template. We'll include suggested reserved sizing given the 40 qps baseline and 300 qps peak you mentioned.
[03:20] Benji Rao: Operationally who owns the autoscale policy? We want the platform team to control policies, not product team. Does Redwood provide RBAC to restrict who can change scaling?
[03:28] Omar Reyes: RBAC is supported in the Console; you can lock scaling config behind roles and audit changes in the activity logs.
[03:35] Liam O'Connor: Network-wise — we run in VPC, we need private connectivity, and CIDR whitelisting for egress. Any options?
[03:41] Maya Chen: Dedicated and Private both support VPC peering and private endpoints; on-prem route is possible but more involved. We'll include a VPC connectivity checklist in the security pack.
[03:50] Priya Nair: For the pilot, what's realistic? We don't want to commit to a year before we validate tail latency and the isolation boundaries.
[03:57] Maya Chen: Typical pilot is 1 week with reserved capacity equivalent to 2 nodes sized for your baseline, Redwood runs benchmark tests and we collect metrics (p95/p99 latencies, throughput, token cost). You can run your sample prompt set against it.
[04:12] Sara Patel: OK that sounds good. We'll need a test harness to reproduce our request patterns.
[04:16] Omar Reyes: We'll provide a load generator and script — we've already got a perf test for 512-token sequences; we'll adapt to your 350–1k distribution.
[04:26] Priya Nair: Any hard SLAs on latency for Dedicated? We need guidance on expected p95 at baseline for 512 tokens.
[04:34] Omar Reyes: SLA is more about availability and throughput; latency SLOs depend on model and node type. For example, an L2GP model on an A100-equivalent node with warm pool, p95 for 512 tokens can be ~120–180ms in many cases. But we'll run your exact model + token distribution in the pilot.
[04:52] Benji Rao: You mentioned model variants — does Redwood manage model hosting or do we bring our own container?
[04:58] Maya Chen: We support both: host curated open models and you can bring your own container or model artifact. For private models we help with onboarding and kernel selection.
[05:07] Liam O'Connor: Compliance point — SOC 2 and ISO audit evidence — is that shareable?
[05:12] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll send a SOC 2 summary and security pack. For deeper checks we coordinate NDAs and a narrower security review.
[05:20] Priya Nair: If we decide private later, what's the on-prem timeline usually?
[05:25] Omar Reyes: On-prem deployments take longer — typically 8–12 weeks for full org install and testing depending on your infra and networking. Dedicated is faster — pilot can be scheduled in days to a week.
[05:36] Sara Patel: A clarification — KV cache isolation, you said logical partitioning. Can tenants share the same in-memory cache with enforced namespaces? We're worried about side channels.
[05:45] Omar Reyes: There are two patterns: logical namespaces for KV caches with RBAC and encryption — lower blast radius but some shared process. Or single-tenant nodes where cache is physically separated. For high-risk tenants we recommend node separation.
[05:59] Benji Rao: Any third-party tools for monitoring? We want traces and token-level cost breakdowns.
[06:05] Maya Chen: Console has token-level cost, traces, and per-route dashboards. You can also export traces to your observability backend (e.g., Datadog, NewRelic).
[06:15] Priya Nair: This is getting into the weeds but who pays for prewarming? If we want the warm pool up, is that included or a separate charge?
[06:22] Omar Reyes: Warm pools are billable — prewarmed capacity is billed as reserved compute to reflect real costs. We provide guidance to size warm pools efficiently.
[06:32] Priya Nair: Ok. On SLAs, can we set up a failover to a lower-cost model if our primary model OOMs?
[06:38] Omar Reyes: Yes — rollout policies allow automatic fallback to compatible model variants or scaled-down modes. Useful for graceful degradation.
[06:46] Liam O'Connor: Any gotchas with quantization and customer-provided models?
[06:51] Omar Reyes: Quantization is often beneficial for TCO but can change outputs. We'll run evals and regression alerts as part of Optimize. For some models, mixed-precision paths are better.
[07:03] Maya Chen: Alright, let's recap and confirm action items. Maya to send pricing + burst template and security pack. Omar to prepare bench plan and load scripts. Priya to share traffic CSV and sample prompts.
[07:15] Priya Nair: Sounds good. We'll try to get the traffic data by Monday. Procurement is also wanting a statement of work for the pilot.
[07:22] Maya Chen: We'll attach a short SOW for the 1-week pilot.
[07:25] Benji Rao: Final question — do you support tenant-level SSO with SCIM provisioning?
[07:30] Maya Chen: Yes, SSO with SAML/OIDC and SCIM provisioning is supported in Console. We'll include the SCIM docs in the security pack.
[07:36] Priya Nair: Great. Thanks everyone.
[07:38] Maya Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up with docs and draft SOW.
[07:41] (call ends)

Transcript notes: occasional misrecognitions ("Anthopic" for Anthropic), filler words, and speaker overlaps. Some product names were transcribed as "Red wood" or "Redwood Ded" in places in the auto notes.
